```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Plain output and no progress bars in the rendered page. Output is 76
# columns wide, so that with knitr's "#> " it fits pkgdown's code box.
options(
  width = 76,
  cli.num_colors = 1,
  cli.dynamic = FALSE,
  cli.progress_show_after = Inf
)
```

`inla_vanilla()` calls `logpost` many times, and without a gradient the
count grows with the square of the number of parameters $m$: the Hessian by
finite differences takes about $m^2$ calls, the skew-normal scans about
$2m^2$, and the VB correction $(m + 1)(m + 2)$ per sweep, over a few sweeps.
For 39 parameters that is over 20,000 calls. Two things help: a faster
`logpost`, and a gradient.

This article does both for a structural equation model (SEM) with 39
parameters. We write the log-posterior in plain R first, then in C++ with
[Rcpp](https://www.rcpp.org/) and
[RcppEigen](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RcppEigen), and then add an
analytic gradient in C++. The article [Using TMB](tmb.html) fits the same
model with a TMB template, which computes the gradient by automatic
differentiation.

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| message: false
library(inlavanilla)
data(PoliticalDemocracy, package = "lavaan")
```

## The model

The `PoliticalDemocracy` data in lavaan come from Bollen (1989). For 75
developing countries they hold three indicators of industrialisation in 1960
(`x1`–`x3`), and the same four indicators of political democracy in 1960
(`y1`–`y4`) and 1965 (`y5`–`y8`). In the lavaan syntax that INLAvaan
takes, the model is:

```{r}
#| label: model
model <- "
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8
"
```

Three latent variables, industrialisation in 1960 (`ind60`) and democracy in
1960 and 1965 (`dem60`, `dem65`), are each measured by their indicators. The
first loading of each is fixed at 1, and the labels `a`, `b` and `c` hold the
1960 and 1965 loadings equal. Democracy in 1960 depends on industrialisation,
and democracy in 1965 on both. The residuals of the same indicator in the two
years are correlated, as are those of `y2` with `y4` and `y6` with `y8`.

With a mean structure, the 11 indicators of each country are normal with mean
$\nu$ and covariance

$$
\Sigma = \Lambda (I - B)^{-1} \Psi (I - B)^{-\top} \Lambda^\top + \Theta,
$$

where $\nu$ holds the 11 intercepts, $\Lambda$ ($11 \times 3$) the loadings,
$B$ ($3 \times 3$) the regressions among the latent variables, $\Psi$ the
diagonal matrix of the variance of `ind60` and the disturbance variances of
`dem60` and `dem65`, and $\Theta$ ($11 \times 11$) the residual covariances.
The log-likelihood is the sum of 75 multivariate normal log-densities.

## Parameters and priors

`inla_vanilla()` needs every parameter on an unconstrained scale. We use the
parameterisation and default priors of
[INLAvaan](https://inlavaan.haziqj.ml/), so the results can be compared with
`INLAvaan::asem(model, PoliticalDemocracy, meanstructure = TRUE)`:

| Parameters | Number | Unconstrained scale | Prior |
|:-----------|-------:|:--------------------|:------|
| Intercepts $\nu$ | 11 | as they are | $N(0, 32^2)$ |
| Loadings (`x2`, `x3`, `a`, `b`, `c`) | 5 | as they are | $N(0, 10^2)$ |
| Regressions | 3 | as they are | $N(0, 10^2)$ |
| Variances (3 latent, 11 residual) | 14 | $\ell = \log \sigma^2$ | $\text{Gamma}(1, \text{rate } 0.5)$ on $\sigma$ |
| Residual covariances | 6 | $z = \operatorname{atanh} \rho$ | $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$ on $(\rho + 1)/2$ |

A residual covariance enters through its correlation $\rho$, as
$\theta_{ij} = \rho \sqrt{\theta_{ii} \theta_{jj}}$, and both its parameter
$z$ and its prior refer to $\rho$.

Two of the priors are on a different scale from the parameter, so `logpost`
needs their log-Jacobians:

* A variance's prior is on its standard deviation
  $\sigma = e^{\ell / 2}$, and $d\sigma / d\ell = \sigma / 2$. Its term in the
  log-posterior is $\log p(\sigma) + \log(\sigma / 2)$.
* A correlation's prior is on $\rho = \tanh z$, and
  $d\rho / dz = 1 - \rho^2$. The Beta(1, 1) prior on $(\rho + 1)/2$ is the
  uniform density $1/2$ on $(-1, 1)$, so the term is
  $\log(1/2) + \log(1 - \rho^2)$.

The normal priors are on the parameters themselves and need none.

## The log-posterior in R

The data, ordered as the rows of $\Lambda$, and the names of the 39
parameters. `logv_` marks a log variance and `z_` a residual correlation on
the atanh scale.

```{r}
#| label: data
ov <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", paste0("y", 1:8))
Y <- as.matrix(PoliticalDemocracy[, ov])

cov_pairs <- rbind(
  c("y1", "y5"),
  c("y2", "y4"),
  c("y2", "y6"),
  c("y3", "y7"),
  c("y4", "y8"),
  c("y6", "y8")
)

parnames <- c(
  paste0("nu_", ov), # 1-11
  c("lam_x2", "lam_x3", "a", "b", "c"), # 12-16
  c("beta_dem60_ind60", "beta_dem65_ind60", "beta_dem65_dem60"), # 17-19
  paste0("logv_", c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")), # 20-22
  paste0("logv_", ov), # 23-33
  paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2]) # 34-39
)
```

The free entries of $\Lambda$, $B$ and $\Theta$, as matrix indices, and the
element of the parameter vector that fills each. The loadings `a`, `b` and
`c` fill two entries each.

```{r}
#| label: layout
lambda_fixed <- matrix(0, 11, 3)
lambda_fixed[cbind(c(1, 4, 8), 1:3)] <- 1
lambda_at <- cbind(c(2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11), rep(1:3, c(2, 3, 3)))
lambda_par <- c(12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 14, 15, 16)
beta_at <- cbind(c(2, 3, 3), c(1, 1, 2))
cov_at <- matrix(match(cov_pairs, ov), ncol = 2)
```

The model-implied covariance matrix, the 75 pointwise log-likelihoods, and
the log-prior with its Jacobians. The log-posterior is their total. Keeping
the pointwise log-likelihood as a function of its own makes it available for
leave-one-out cross-validation.

```{r}
#| label: logpost-r
implied_cov <- function(theta) {
  Lambda <- lambda_fixed
  Lambda[lambda_at] <- theta[lambda_par]
  B <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  B[beta_at] <- theta[17:19]
  psi <- exp(theta[20:22])
  v <- exp(theta[23:33])
  Theta <- diag(v)
  Theta[cov_at] <- tanh(theta[34:39]) * sqrt(v[cov_at[, 1]] * v[cov_at[, 2]])
  Theta[cov_at[, 2:1]] <- Theta[cov_at]
  LA <- Lambda %*% solve(diag(3) - B)
  LA %*% (psi * t(LA)) + Theta # LA Psi LA' + Theta
}

loglik_r <- function(theta, Y) {
  Sigma <- implied_cov(theta)
  R <- tryCatch(chol(Sigma), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(R)) {
    return(rep(-Inf, nrow(Y))) # Sigma is not positive definite
  }
  Z <- backsolve(R, t(Y) - theta[1:11], transpose = TRUE)
  -0.5 * ncol(Y) * log(2 * pi) - sum(log(diag(R))) - 0.5 * colSums(Z^2)
}

logprior_r <- function(theta) {
  logv <- theta[20:33]
  sd <- exp(logv / 2)
  rho <- tanh(theta[34:39])
  sum(dnorm(theta[1:11], 0, 32, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dnorm(theta[12:19], 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dgamma(sd, shape = 1, rate = 0.5, log = TRUE) + log(sd / 2)) +
    sum(dbeta((rho + 1) / 2, 1, 1, log = TRUE) - log(2) + log1p(-rho^2))
}

logpost_r <- function(theta, Y) {
  sum(loglik_r(theta, Y)) + logprior_r(theta)
}
```

Starting values: the sample means for the intercepts, loadings of 1, no
regressions, half of each sample variance for the residual variances, and no
residual correlations.

```{r}
#| label: init
init <- c(
  colMeans(Y),
  rep(1, 5),
  rep(0, 3),
  rep(0, 3),
  log(apply(Y, 2, var) / 2),
  rep(0, 6)
)
names(init) <- parnames
```

### A check against INLAvaan

INLAvaan fits the same model, with the same parameterisation and priors:

```{r}
#| label: inlavaan
fit_inlavaan <- INLAvaan::asem(
  model,
  PoliticalDemocracy,
  meanstructure = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
int <- INLAvaan::get_inlavaan_internal(fit_inlavaan)
```

Its parameters are ours, in another order and under lavaan's names. Here is
its posterior mode in our order:

```{r}
#| label: inlavaan-mode
lv <- c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")
inlavaan_names <- c(
  paste0(ov, "~1"),
  "ind60=~x2",
  "ind60=~x3",
  "a",
  "b",
  "c",
  "dem60~ind60",
  "dem65~ind60",
  "dem65~dem60",
  paste0(c(lv, ov), "~~", c(lv, ov)),
  paste0(cov_pairs[, 1], "~~", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
at <- match(inlavaan_names, names(int$coefficients))
theta_inlavaan <- setNames(int$theta_star_novbc[at], parnames)
```

There, our log-posterior should equal INLAvaan's, which its optimiser
minimised as the negative:

```{r}
#| label: inlavaan-check
c(ours = logpost_r(theta_inlavaan, Y), INLAvaan = -int$opt$objective)
```

### How long R takes

A helper to time one call, in microseconds:

```{r}
#| label: timer
time_per_call <- function(f, n) {
  elapsed <- system.time(
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      f()
    }
  )[["elapsed"]]
  1e6 * elapsed / n
}
us_r <- time_per_call(function() logpost_r(init, Y), n = 1000)
us_r
```

With `vb = FALSE`, `inla_vanilla()` skips the VB correction and runs only the
mode search and the skew-normal marginals:

```{r}
#| label: fit-r
fit_r <- inla_vanilla(logpost_r, init, Y = Y, vb = FALSE)
fit_r$counts
```

These two stages take
`r format(fit_r$counts[["logpost"]], big.mark = ",")` calls. The VB
correction would add $(m + 1)(m + 2) = 1{,}640$ calls per sweep, over a few
sweeps: without a gradient it takes the expected gradient from values of
`logpost` alone. We come back to the cost of a full fit below.

## The log-posterior in C++

The C++ version mirrors the R one. RcppEigen provides the matrix algebra and
converts R's numeric vectors and matrices to Eigen's `VectorXd` and
`MatrixXd` (an `Eigen::Map` reuses R's memory instead of copying). The C++
file starts with the layout of the parameter vector, now with indices from 0,
and a function that builds the model matrices.

```{r}
#| label: cpp-file
cpp_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "sem.cpp")
```

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = cpp_file, lang = "cpp")}
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEigen)]]
#include <RcppEigen.h>

using Eigen::Map;
using Eigen::MatrixXd;
using Eigen::VectorXd;

// theta: intercepts 0-10, loadings 11-15, regressions 16-18, latent log
// variances 19-21, residual log variances 22-32, residual correlations
// (atanh scale) 33-38. Indicators in the order x1, x2, x3, y1, ..., y8.

// Free loadings: row and column of Lambda, and the element of theta
const int lambda_row[8] = {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10};
const int lambda_col[8] = {0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2};
const int lambda_par[8] = {11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 13, 14, 15};
// Regressions: dem60 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ dem60
const int beta_row[3] = {1, 2, 2};
const int beta_col[3] = {0, 0, 1};
// Residual covariances: y1-y5, y2-y4, y2-y6, y3-y7, y4-y8, y6-y8
const int cov_i[6] = {3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8};
const int cov_j[6] = {7, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10};

struct Sem {
  VectorXd nu, psi, v, rho;
  MatrixXd Lambda, A, M, Theta, Sigma;  // A = (I - B)^-1, M = A Psi A'
};

Sem sem_matrices(const VectorXd& theta) {
  Sem s;
  s.nu = theta.head(11);
  s.Lambda = MatrixXd::Zero(11, 3);
  s.Lambda(0, 0) = s.Lambda(3, 1) = s.Lambda(7, 2) = 1;
  for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    s.Lambda(lambda_row[k], lambda_col[k]) = theta[lambda_par[k]];
  }
  MatrixXd B = MatrixXd::Zero(3, 3);
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) B(beta_row[k], beta_col[k]) = theta[16 + k];
  s.A = (MatrixXd::Identity(3, 3) - B).inverse();
  s.psi = theta.segment(19, 3).array().exp();
  s.v = theta.segment(22, 11).array().exp();
  s.rho = theta.segment(33, 6).array().tanh();
  s.Theta = s.v.asDiagonal();
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    int i = cov_i[k], j = cov_j[k];
    s.Theta(i, j) = s.Theta(j, i) = s.rho[k] * std::sqrt(s.v[i] * s.v[j]);
  }
  s.M = s.A * s.psi.asDiagonal() * s.A.transpose();
  s.Sigma = s.Lambda * s.M * s.Lambda.transpose() + s.Theta;
  return s;
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
VectorXd loglik_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  Sem s = sem_matrices(theta);
  Eigen::LLT<MatrixXd> llt(s.Sigma);
  if (llt.info() != Eigen::Success) {  // Sigma is not positive definite
    return VectorXd::Constant(Y.rows(), R_NegInf);
  }
  MatrixXd D = Y.rowwise() - s.nu.transpose();
  MatrixXd Z = llt.matrixL().solve(D.transpose());
  // matrixLLT() holds L, whose diagonal gives half the log-determinant
  double half_logdet = llt.matrixLLT().diagonal().array().log().sum();
  double c = -0.5 * Y.cols() * std::log(2 * M_PI) - half_logdet;
  return (c - 0.5 * Z.colwise().squaredNorm().array()).matrix().transpose();
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
double logprior_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta) {
  double lp = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) lp += R::dnorm(theta[i], 0, 32, true);
  for (int i = 11; i < 19; i++) lp += R::dnorm(theta[i], 0, 10, true);
  for (int i = 19; i < 33; i++) {
    double sd = std::exp(theta[i] / 2);
    // R::dgamma() takes the scale, 1 / rate
    lp += R::dgamma(sd, 1, 1 / 0.5, true) + std::log(sd / 2);
  }
  for (int i = 33; i < 39; i++) {
    double rho = std::tanh(theta[i]);
    lp += R::dbeta((rho + 1) / 2, 1, 1, true) - std::log(2.0) +
      std::log1p(-rho * rho);
  }
  return lp;
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
double logpost_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  return loglik_cpp(theta, Y).sum() + logprior_cpp(theta);
}
```

### The gradient

The gradient follows from the chain rule, and costs about as much as the
log-likelihood itself. Write $D$ for the $n \times 11$ matrix of data minus
$\nu$ and $\Omega = \Sigma^{-1}$. The derivative of the log-likelihood is
$\Omega D^\top \mathbf{1}$ with respect to $\nu$, and

$$
G = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \Omega D^\top D \, \Omega - n \Omega \right)
$$

with respect to $\Sigma$. Through
$\Sigma = \Lambda M \Lambda^\top + \Theta$, with $A = (I - B)^{-1}$ and
$M = A \Psi A^\top$, the derivatives with respect to the model matrices are

$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \Lambda} = 2 G \Lambda M, \qquad
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial B} = 2 A^\top \Lambda^\top G \Lambda M, \qquad
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \Psi} = A^\top \Lambda^\top G \Lambda A,
$$

and $G_{ii}$ for a residual variance $\theta_{ii}$ and $2 G_{ij}$ for a
residual covariance. A loading held equal across years sums its two entries.
On the unconstrained scale, a log variance multiplies its derivative by the
variance. A residual covariance
$\theta_{ij} = \rho \sqrt{\theta_{ii} \theta_{jj}}$ moves with $z$, through
$d\theta_{ij} / dz = (1 - \rho^2) \sqrt{\theta_{ii} \theta_{jj}}$, and with
both log variances, through $d\theta_{ij} / d\ell_i = \theta_{ij} / 2$.

The log-prior adds $-\vartheta / s^2$ for each normal prior,
$1/2 - \sigma / 4$ for each log variance and $-2\rho$ for each correlation.
We append the gradient to the same file:

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = cpp_file, lang = "cpp", append = TRUE)}
// Gradient of logpost_cpp() with respect to theta
// [[Rcpp::export]]
VectorXd grad_cpp(const Map<VectorXd> theta, const Map<MatrixXd> Y) {
  Sem s = sem_matrices(theta);
  Eigen::LLT<MatrixXd> llt(s.Sigma);
  if (llt.info() != Eigen::Success) return VectorXd::Constant(39, NA_REAL);
  VectorXd g = VectorXd::Zero(39);

  // Log-likelihood, through G = d loglik / d Sigma
  int n = Y.rows();
  MatrixXd Omega = llt.solve(MatrixXd::Identity(11, 11));
  MatrixXd OD = Omega * (Y.rowwise() - s.nu.transpose()).transpose();
  MatrixXd G = 0.5 * (OD * OD.transpose() - n * Omega);

  g.head(11) = OD.rowwise().sum();
  MatrixXd dLambda = 2 * G * s.Lambda * s.M;
  for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    g[lambda_par[k]] += dLambda(lambda_row[k], lambda_col[k]);
  }
  MatrixXd LGL = s.Lambda.transpose() * G * s.Lambda;
  MatrixXd dB = 2 * s.A.transpose() * LGL * s.M;
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) g[16 + k] = dB(beta_row[k], beta_col[k]);
  MatrixXd dPsi = s.A.transpose() * LGL * s.A;
  for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) g[19 + k] = dPsi(k, k) * s.psi[k];
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) g[22 + i] = G(i, i) * s.v[i];
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    int i = cov_i[k], j = cov_j[k];
    g[22 + i] += G(i, j) * s.Theta(i, j);
    g[22 + j] += G(i, j) * s.Theta(i, j);
    g[33 + k] = 2 * G(i, j) * (1 - s.rho[k] * s.rho[k]) *
      std::sqrt(s.v[i] * s.v[j]);
  }

  // Log-prior, with the Jacobians
  for (int i = 0; i < 11; i++) g[i] -= theta[i] / (32.0 * 32.0);
  for (int i = 11; i < 19; i++) g[i] -= theta[i] / (10.0 * 10.0);
  for (int i = 19; i < 33; i++) g[i] += 0.5 - std::exp(theta[i] / 2) / 4;
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) g[33 + k] -= 2 * s.rho[k];
  return g;
}
```

### Compiling and checking

`Rcpp::sourceCpp()` compiles the file and defines the four exported functions
in R. (`Rcpp::sourceCpp(code = ...)` takes the same code as a string.)

```{r}
#| label: compile
#| message: false
Rcpp::sourceCpp(cpp_file)
```

The C++ log-posterior should match the R one to rounding error, at the
starting values, at INLAvaan's posterior mode and at some random points:

```{r}
#| label: check-cpp
set.seed(1)
points <- c(
  list(init, theta_inlavaan),
  replicate(4, init + rnorm(39, sd = 0.3), simplify = FALSE)
)
vapply(points, function(th) logpost_cpp(th, Y) - logpost_r(th, Y), 0)
max(abs(loglik_cpp(theta_inlavaan, Y) - loglik_r(theta_inlavaan, Y)))
```

The gradient should match central differences of the R log-posterior, up to
their own error, about $10^{-8}$ relative:

```{r}
#| label: check-grad
fd_grad <- function(f, x, h = 1e-5) {
  vapply(
    seq_along(x),
    function(j) {
      e <- replace(numeric(length(x)), j, h)
      (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h)
    },
    0
  )
}
vapply(
  points,
  function(th) {
    g_fd <- fd_grad(function(x) logpost_r(x, Y), th)
    max(abs(grad_cpp(th, Y) - g_fd) / (1 + abs(g_fd)))
  },
  0
)
```

## Speed

Per call, in microseconds:

```{r}
#| label: speed
us_cpp <- time_per_call(function() logpost_cpp(init, Y), n = 10000)
us_grad <- time_per_call(function() grad_cpp(init, Y), n = 10000)
c(R = us_r, `C++` = us_cpp, `C++ gradient` = us_grad)
```

The C++ log-posterior is about `r round(us_r / us_cpp)` times faster than
the R one, and the analytic gradient costs about the same as one
log-posterior, where finite differences need 40.

Now the full fit, with the VB correction, first without a gradient:

```{r}
#| label: fit-cpp
fit_cpp <- inla_vanilla(logpost_cpp, init, Y = Y)
```

It took `r format(fit_cpp$counts[["logpost"]], big.mark = ",")` calls. In R,
at `r round(us_r)` microseconds a call, these would take about
`r round(fit_cpp$counts[["logpost"]] * us_r / 1e6, 1)` seconds. With the
gradient:

```{r}
#| label: fit-grad
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost_cpp, init, grad = grad_cpp, Y = Y)
```

`inla_vanilla()` checks the gradient against finite differences at `init`,
and its Jacobian at the mode for symmetry, and warns if either check fails.
Here neither does. The calls and times (in seconds) of the three fits:

```{r}
#| label: fit-table
fits <- list(`R, no VB` = fit_r, `C++` = fit_cpp, `C++ and gradient` = fit)
t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$counts, round(f$timing, 2))))
```

The VB correction takes the same nodes either way: the gradient at
$(m + 1)(m + 2) + 1 = 1{,}641$ points per sweep, or `logpost` at all but the
centre. The gradient buys accuracy there: its VB mean is exact when the
log-posterior is a polynomial of degree six, against degree four from
`logpost` alone.

The three fits agree. The skew-normal marginals do not depend on the VB
correction, so even `fit_r` gives the same table. The largest difference in a
posterior mean or quantile, in posterior SDs:

```{r}
#| label: fit-agree
sds <- fit$summary[, "SD"]
c(
  R = max(abs(fit_r$summary - fit$summary) / sds),
  `C++` = max(abs(fit_cpp$summary - fit$summary) / sds)
)
```

## Results

```{r}
#| label: summary
summary(fit)
```

The intercepts are close to symmetric, and the loadings and regressions are
mildly right-skewed. The most skewed marginal is that of the disturbance
variance of `dem65`. Democracy in 1960 and industrialisation explain most of
the variation in democracy in 1965 (see $R^2$ below), so this variance is
small and poorly determined, and its log has a long left tail. `summary()`
flags it twice: the straight scan through the mode misses enough
log-density that its marginal may come out too narrow, and its skew-normal
and VB means differ by 0.2 posterior SDs, another sign that the marginal is
hard to approximate.

Here the flags are borne out. Checked against MCMC, the marginals of
`logv_dem65` and `logv_x2` are less than half as wide as the posterior, with
the 2.5% quantile of `logv_dem65` at −3.6 against −7.3. The data cannot rule
out a variance near zero, so on the log scale the posterior has a long
exponential left tail, held back only by the prior, and a skew-normal cannot
follow it. On the variance scale, where the tail near zero is compressed, the
error is much smaller: the posterior means of the two variances are 0.2
posterior SDs too high. No check flags `logv_x2`: its ridge bends less,
and none of the checks is aimed at a tail like this. The other 37 marginals
agree with MCMC to within 7% in SD.

```{r}
#| label: plot
#| fig-alt: "Posterior densities of three parameters: the two regressions of 1965 democracy, both slightly right-skewed, and the log disturbance variance of 1965 democracy, strongly left-skewed. Dashed Gaussian curves are symmetric."
plot(fit, pars = c("beta_dem65_ind60", "beta_dem65_dem60", "logv_dem65"))
```

### Derived quantities

`sampling()` gives draws of any function of the parameters. Industrialisation
affects democracy in 1965 directly, and indirectly through democracy in
1960. The indirect effect is a product of two regressions:

```{r}
#| label: effects
set.seed(2026)
effects <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 10000, fun = function(theta) {
  direct <- theta[["beta_dem65_ind60"]]
  indirect <- theta[["beta_dem60_ind60"]] * theta[["beta_dem65_dem60"]]
  c(direct = direct, indirect = indirect, total = direct + indirect)
})
round(t(apply(effects, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))), 3)
```

The share of the variance of `dem65` explained by industrialisation and
democracy in 1960, $R^2$, needs the covariance matrix of the latent
variables, $A \Psi A^\top$:

```{r}
#| label: r2
r2_dem65 <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 10000, fun = function(theta) {
  B <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  B[beta_at] <- theta[17:19]
  A <- solve(diag(3) - B)
  M <- A %*% diag(exp(theta[20:22])) %*% t(A)
  1 - exp(theta[["logv_dem65"]]) / M[3, 3]
})
round(quantile(r2_dem65, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)), 3)
```

### Compared with INLAvaan

INLAvaan runs the same approximation on the same log-posterior, so the two
fits should agree. The modes and the Laplace covariances, in posterior SDs and
relative to the largest covariance:

```{r}
#| label: vs-inlavaan
sds <- sqrt(diag(fit$cov))
c(
  mode = max(abs(theta_inlavaan - fit$mode) / sds),
  cov = max(abs(int$Sigma_theta[at, at] - fit$cov)) / max(abs(fit$cov))
)
```

Both agree to a few parts in $10^{4}$, the precision of the two optimisers
and finite-difference Hessians.

INLAvaan fits a skew-normal to each parameter as well. Its means and SDs, on
the same scale, next to ours for the regressions and the variance of `dem65`:

```{r}
#| label: vs-inlavaan-marginals
sn <- int$approx_data[inlavaan_names, ]
delta <- sn[, "alpha"] / sqrt(1 + sn[, "alpha"]^2)
sn_mean <- sn[, "xi"] + sn[, "omega"] * delta * sqrt(2 / pi)
sn_sd <- sn[, "omega"] * sqrt(1 - 2 * delta^2 / pi)
names(sn_mean) <- names(sn_sd) <- parnames

pars <- c(parnames[17:19], "logv_dem65")
round(
  cbind(
    `mean, INLAvaan` = sn_mean[pars],
    `mean, ours` = fit$summary[pars, "Mean"],
    `SD, INLAvaan` = sn_sd[pars],
    `SD, ours` = fit$summary[pars, "SD"]
  ),
  4
)
max(abs(sn_mean - fit$summary[, "Mean"]) / fit$summary[, "SD"])
```

Over all 39 parameters, the means differ by at most about $10^{-4}$
posterior SDs. The two packages share the skew-normal marginals, and with
them the limitation for `logv_dem65` and `logv_x2` described above.

The log marginal likelihoods share their Laplace part. The VB terms differ a
little, because INLAvaan takes the expectation in the VB correction with 64
Sobol points and inlavanilla with a deterministic cubature rule:

```{r}
#| label: vs-inlavaan-logml
round(
  rbind(
    INLAvaan = c(
      Laplace = int$mloglik - int$vb$kld_global,
      VB = int$vb$kld_global,
      total = int$mloglik
    ),
    ours = c(
      Laplace = fit$logml_laplace,
      VB = fit$logml - fit$logml_laplace,
      total = fit$logml
    )
  ),
  3
)
```

The Laplace parts agree to the last digit. The VB terms differ by
`r round(int$vb$kld_global - (fit$logml - fit$logml_laplace), 2)`, from the
two integration rules: 64 Sobol points estimate the expectation with Monte
Carlo error, which the deterministic cubature rule avoids.

## References

Bollen, K. A. (1989). *Structural equations with latent variables*. Wiley.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179>
